new.title: Step into the baroque church of Saint-Loup
new.desc: The Jesuits arrived in Namur in 1610 and had Brother Pierre Huyssens, a master of Belgian baroque, design this church for their college. Building began in 1621 and dragged on for twenty years for lack of money, with the consecration following in 1645.
new.tip: The church is not open all day, so try the afternoon or look out for a concert. It is a short walk from the belfry.
new.q: Église Saint-Loup Rue du Collège Namur

new.title: Work through the beer list at Le Chapitre
new.desc: Tucked behind Saint-Aubain cathedral on Rue du Séminaire, Le Chapitre is known as the historic beer bar of Namur. The list runs through Trappists and speciality beers, served in an eccentrically decorated room or on a shaded terrace.
new.tip: It stays open late and gets lively in the evening; come in the late afternoon for a quiet table outside.
new.q: Le Chapitre Rue du Séminaire 4 Namur

new.title: Follow the smell of coffee to Delahaut
new.desc: Léon Delahaut founded this family coffee roaster in Namur in 1864, and the name has been part of the city ever since. The roasting itself has moved out to Suarlée, but the shop on Rue de l'Ange still sells the house coffees in the heart of town.
new.tip: Ask what was roasted most recently and have it ground for your machine at home. It is a handy stop between the belfry and the Sambre.

new.title: Train your nose at the Delforge perfume workshop
new.desc: Inside the citadel, the Delforge perfume house composes and matures its fragrances in a listed building and its underground galleries. The hour-long visit takes in a film, the workshop, the perfumer's organ of essences, the maceration gallery and a room where you test scents.
new.tip: Guided visits for individuals are on Saturdays at 3.30 pm, and from Monday to Saturday in school holidays; they cost only a few euros but must be booked.
new.q: Parfums Guy Delforge Route Merveilleuse 60 Namur

new.title: Relive the Battle of the Bulge in Bastogne
new.desc: In the winter of 1944 the American 101st Airborne Division held the crossroads town of Bastogne against the last great German offensive. The Bastogne War Museum on Mardasson hill tells the story in an interactive way, right beside the star-shaped Mardasson memorial, inaugurated in 1950 to thank the American soldiers.
new.tip: The museum is usually open daily and deserves two to three hours. Bastogne has no railway station, so take the bus from Libramont if you are not driving.
new.q: Bastogne War Museum Colline du Mardasson 5 Bastogne

new.title: Eat at Wagon Léo on Bastogne's main square
new.desc: Léo has been feeding Bastogne since 1946 and is described as the oldest restaurant still working in town. Today it is a bistro and restaurant on Place McAuliffe serving classic dishes, seasonal specials and oysters.
new.tip: The bistro side is the one for a quick plate and a drink on the terrace. Book at weekends, when battlefield visitors fill the square.

new.title: Find the foxholes in the Bois Jacques
new.desc: In the wood near the village of Foy, north of Bastogne, the foxholes dug by American paratroopers of Easy Company in the winter of 1944 are still visible in the forest floor. The wood is now looked after as a battlefield site linked to the Bastogne War Museum.
new.tip: Go early or late in the day, when the place is quiet. Stay on the paths and leave the foxholes as you find them.
new.q: The Easy Company Foxholes Foy Bastogne

new.title: Climb the 408 steps to the citadel of Dinant
new.desc: The fortress on the cliff above Dinant was built in 1818 under Dutch rule, on the site of earlier strongholds going back to a castle of 1051 raised for the Prince-Bishop of Liège. It was sold to the town in 1878 and is now a museum, with a sheer view down on the collegiate church and the Meuse.
new.tip: Take the cable car up and the 408 steps down to save your legs. Go early in high season to avoid the queue.

new.title: Drop in on Monsieur Sax in Dinant
new.desc: Adolphe Sax, who gave the world the saxophone, was born in Dinant on 6 November 1814. A small free museum on the street that bears his name is devoted to him, and a trail through the town keeps his memory alive.
new.tip: It takes only a short while, so it fits easily between the collegiate church and a couque shop.
new.q: La Maison de Monsieur Sax Rue Adolphe Sax Dinant

new.title: Pedal a rail-bike up the Molignée valley
new.desc: An old railway line along the little Molignée river now carries draisines, carts that you pedal along the rails. From the former station of Falaën it is a 6 km round trip to Maredsous station, with a one kilometre walk up to the abbey if you want it.
new.tip: Departures run at fixed times, usually every two hours from late morning, so book ahead and arrive early. Check the season before you go, as winter running is limited.
new.q: Draisines de la Molignée Gare de Falaën

new.title: Lunch on abbey bread, cheese and beer at Floreffe
new.desc: Norbert of Gennep, founder of the Premonstratensian order, established Floreffe abbey in 1121 at the request of the counts of Namur, and the priory of Leffe was one of its foundations. In the abbey's old mill and brewery you can order the abbey's own bread, cheese and beer, indoors or on the terrace.
new.tip: Hot dishes are served at lunchtime from Wednesday to Sunday. Buy the small guide booklet at the counter and walk around the abbey grounds afterwards.

new.title: See the towers of the Château de Vêves
new.desc: Vêves stands above the village of Celles, near a small tributary of the Lesse. The Beaufort family rebuilt it as a strong fortress in 1220, and their descendants, the Liedekerke-Beaufort, restored it in the 18th century and gave it the look it has today.
new.tip: The village of Celles just below is worth the short detour. Check opening days outside summer before you set out.

new.title: Drink a Chouffe in the village where it was born
new.desc: Two brothers-in-law, Pierre Gobron and Christian Bauweraerts, brewed their first 49 litres in the tiny Ardennes village of Achouffe on 27 August 1982. Their gnome is now known far beyond Belgium and the brewery belongs to the Duvel Moortgat group, but the beer is still made here, near Houffalize.
new.tip: Book brewery tours in advance. Forest walks start in the village if you want to earn the second glass.

new.title: Play astronaut at the Euro Space Center
new.desc: The European Space Agency set up a satellite tracking station at Redu in 1968, and the enthusiasm it stirred locally led to this space centre at Transinne, opened in 1991. It mixes exhibitions with hands-on attractions designed to make space science accessible to everyone.
new.tip: It sits right beside the E411 motorway, so it is an easy stop on the way to or from the Ardennes. Book ahead in school holidays.

new.title: Stand at the north gate of Hougoumont
new.desc: This walled farm anchored Wellington's right flank at Waterloo and was fought over all day. When French soldiers broke in through the north gate, a handful of defenders forced it shut again, and Wellington later said the success of the battle turned on the closing of those gates. The farm was restored and reopened on the 200th anniversary in 2015.
new.tip: A sculpture of two soldiers heaving the gate shut stands beside the north entrance. The chapel is the only part of the main house that survived the fire.

new.title: Walk the woods and ponds of the Domaine Solvay
new.desc: The Solvay estate at La Hulpe, named after the industrialist Ernest Solvay, is a public park of 227 hectares of woods, lawns and ponds. More than 450 species of wild plants have been recorded here, along with many remarkable trees.
new.tip: The park is free to enter. Come on a weekday morning to have the paths around the ponds almost to yourself.
